description: A high-contrast timeline of U.S. electricity generation (2007–2026). Watch coal collapse while solar and wind explode — with natural gas and nuclear holding the middle ground. Data in terawatt-hours (TWh); 2025–2026 are marked estimates.
youtube_description:
Gridfront: Coal vs Sun & Wind — 2007 to 2026 (TWh)

Chapters:
00:00 Intro — Why this race matters
00:18 Baseline — 2007: Coal rules the grid (2,016 TWh)
00:45 The early rise of gas & wind (2008–2014)
01:15 The tipping point — gas overtakes coal (2016)
01:42 Solar breakout — growth from ~1 TWh to ~480 TWh (2007–2024)
02:10 Coal collapse — from ~2,016 TWh (2007) to ~610 TWh (2024)
02:40 Nuclear & the steady middle
03:00 Projections to 2026 — renewables ramp while coal fades (estimates)
03:25 Summary & implications for policy, jobs, and reliability
03:55 Sources & further reading
04:15 Subscribe & follow for more chart-race explainers

What you’re seeing: annual generation in terawatt-hours (TWh) for major U.S. electricity sources. Coal falls dramatically from ~2,016 TWh in 2007 to ~610 TWh in 2024; solar grows from ~1 TWh to ~480 TWh in the same period. Natural gas climbs and fluctuates around 1,200–1,700 TWh. Wind climbs steadily to the 400–500 TWh range. Nuclear remains relatively flat near ~770–810 TWh.

Key sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) annual electricity generation reports, EPA analyses of generation trends, IEA country profiles, and publicly released annual reports from grid operators. Specific datasets used: EIA Electric Power Annual and Monthly generation-by-source time series (2007–2024). 2025–2026 values are labeled as estimates based on recent build rates and EIA short-term projections.

instagram_caption:
⚡️ The U.S. power grid's cinematic collapse and rise — in one scroll. 

In 2007 coal generated roughly 2,016 TWh of U.S. electricity. By 2024 that figure had plunged to ~610 TWh — a two-thirds collapse in under two decades. Meanwhile, solar rose from essentially 1 TWh in 2007 to ~480 TWh by 2024. Wind, once a niche, climbed from ~15 TWh to ~440 TWh. Natural gas moved from ~1,230 TWh to the 1,600–1,700 TWh band and became the swing source that replaced a chunk of coal. Nuclear stayed stubbornly stable around ~770–810 TWh. 

This timeline tells a brutal, clear story: one fuel (coal) crashed, two technologies (solar and wind) sprinted, and natural gas filled the gap. Key turning points: around 2015–2016 gas surpassed coal as the largest single source; 2016 onward marks the steep decline of coal plants and the rapid build-out of utility-scale solar and wind. The result is a fundamentally different grid mix with major implications for jobs, policy, emissions, and grid planning.

Numbers matter: from ~2,016 TWh of coal in 2007 to ~610 TWh in 2024; solar grew from ~1 TWh to ~480 TWh in the same span. Those aren't small swings — they're system-level tectonic change. Projections to 2026 (marked as estimates) show solar potentially hitting ~650 TWh and wind approaching ~500 TWh as retirements and new builds continue.
